bullets: description: Research Brief — original, data-driven public health research using rigorous quantitative methods. Peer-reviewed; same quality, importance and rigor as a Research Article but narrower in scope.
description: Intended for a limited set of key findings or health outcomes that can be shown clearly with only 1 table or 1 figure.
description: Not for pilot, feasibility or developmental studies, convenience-sampled data, or preliminary results — those may fit the Practice Evaluation format instead.
limits: main text ≤ 1200 words (excludes abstract, citations, tables and figures).
limits: structured abstract ≤ 180 words, including its headings.
limits: 1 figure, image and/or table in total.
limits: ≤ 12 references (AMA Manual of Style, 10th edition).
limits: cover letter ≤ 150 words.
limits: supplemental files ≤ 10 pages; where possible 1–4 tables/figures plus syntax, code or study methods.
limits: excess references cost $300 per 1–50 over the cap, or list the nonessential ones unnumbered by topic in an online-only appendix.
components: title page (separate file) — manuscript title, author names, author affiliations, and the full abstract.
components: blinded manuscript file — title and abstract, page numbers, continuous line numbers, and tables/figures either embedded at the end or uploaded separately.

components: structured abstract with formal headings Objectives (begins with "To"), Methods, Results, Conclusions, and Public Health Implications. No Background heading. Must state the date(s) and location(s) of the data.
components: main text with formal subheadings and separate sections for Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and Public Health Implications (practice, policy and research).
components: cover letter — whether the article was commissioned, whether it responds to a call for papers, and anything else relevant to triage. Trial registration date and NCT number go here ONLY.

components: tables — only those summarizing the main findings; simple and self-contained; title gives content, place and time; statistical techniques in the footnotes, not the title; at most 1 column head per column.

components: figures — a single readable, well-described panel (2 panels only for a direct comparison sharing at least 1 axis); title gives content, place and time; black-and-white graphs at most 4 lines, points shown, legend inside the graphic area.
components: images and photos — 300 dpi minimum with a 150-line screen (cover photos 11×17 or larger).
components: supplemental files — online only, blinded, converted to PDF for review.
format: 1.5 or double spacing, 12-point type.
format: continuous line numbers throughout the text (Word: Page Setup > Line Numbers > Continuous).
format: page numbers throughout.

format: the manuscript file must be blinded — no acknowledgements, author information, affiliations or contributions, conflict disclosures, funding sources, IRB institution names, or trial registration number; file names must not carry author names or initials.
format: avoid abbreviations and acronyms; where unavoidable, define clearly after first use.
format: references in AMA Manual of Style, 10th edition.

format: statistics — one decimal place for proportions and effect measures; β becomes b (unstandardized) or B (standardized); report exponentiated estimates (odds ratio, incidence rate ratio) with 95% CIs rather than parameter estimates; P values are unnecessary alongside 95% CIs; report actual P rounded to 2 decimals, never "NS"; 2-sided tests are the rule; P > .05 is not significant.
format: color figures and images incur a publication cost if the article is accepted.
extra: AJPH prioritizes the most recent data available — preferably analyzed within the last 3 years.
extra: a health equity perspective is prioritized (structural and social drivers of health, or variation by population characteristics).
extra: quantitative work should analyze representative local, state or national data, or multi-cohort studies with documented sampling design.
extra: preference for intervention, observational or quasi-experimental studies with direct implications for national public health policy and practice.
extra: studies of population health outcomes or major health care encounters are especially welcome; ecological studies, or studies limited to knowledge and attitudes, are generally not favored.
extra: "nothing about us without us" — studies with at least 1 author from the community or country studied are favored.
extra: non-US studies should make their relevance to global health, or to US public health, explicit.
extra: if a submission does not meet these priorities, justify it in the cover letter.
extra: submit through editorialmanager.com/ajph — submissions sent to an email address are not accepted.
extra: reproduced material must be identified as such and cited, with permissions secured by the authors before final files are uploaded.
